strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding: repeated stimuli and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate estimates of generalization to unseen content.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is a useful evaluation target. The bipartite-graph formulation and story-level grouping for fMRI provide an understandable approach to constructing such splits.

Examines two public datasets covering EEG and fMRI and re-evaluates two established decoding models. Four seeds are reported for overlap statistics, and the appendix supplies several training settings.
weaknesses: The central claim conflates data leakage with different generalization targets. Training and testing on different recordings from the same subject can legitimately evaluate personalized decoding; holding out subjects while retaining stimuli evaluates another setting. Neither automatically means test recordings leaked into training. The proposed joint holdout is valuable, but the claim that all alternative protocols are invalid is insufficiently justified.

The published algorithms do not enforce the advertised separation. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership when restoring edges but does not exclude validation/test stimuli. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks task membership but does not exclude validation/test subjects. Even a two-subject, two-stimulus example can therefore reintroduce overlap. These conditions contradict the prose and leave the reported zero-leakage results unverifiable from the supplied procedure.

The leakage metrics need correction or substantially clearer definitions. Equation 8 counts identical signal instances in the train/test intersection, whereas the conceptual definition concerns different recordings sharing a subject. It also divides by the training count, despite describing a percentage of test signals, and becomes undefined for subjects absent from training. These discrepancies undermine interpretation of Table 1.

Several reported ROUGE results are internally inconsistent. In Table 4, EEG2Text has precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F-score 25.74; this is incompatible with standard F1 computation or consistently averaged per-example F1. Similar violations occur in Table 3. The metric implementation, aggregation, and tables require an audit before the benchmark results can be trusted.

The experiments do not establish the claimed causal effects on encoders and decoders. Falling validation loss or improving test scores over training are not themselves evidence of leakage or overfitting. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together. Controlled comparisons with matched training budgets and data quantities, plus text-only or shuffled-signal controls, are needed to substantiate memorization and the claimed limited contribution of brain signals.

Benchmark reproducibility and the claimed data-utilization benefit remain inadequately supported. The manuscript provides no split-manifest or implementation link, retained/discarded sample counts, final subject/story allocations, or uncertainty estimates for decoding results. Generation-time access to reference prefixes is also unspecified. Assigning graph nodes in an 80:10:10 ratio does not guarantee that ratio for retained samples. Correcting the algorithm and metrics and documenting reproducible, controlled evaluations are necessary before a positive Findings recommendation; these appear addressable in a next-cycle revision.
